passage: Supervisor's note, new trainee check-in Ira joined our Pune office three weeks ago from a small town. Her work is careful and quick. But I've noticed a few things. She often takes long breaks in the stairwell. Twice in meetings her breathing looked fast and shallow, and her hands were gripping the table. When I ask how she is, she says "All good!" too brightly. What I did next: I asked her for a quiet word in an empty meeting room. I said I wasn't worried about her work, only about her. After a long pause she said her thoughts race at night and her chest goes tight, and she's scared she won't cope here. I thanked her for telling me. I gave her the number for the company's counselling service and suggested a check-up with a doctor too. She booked both before she left. - Darshan

qa.q: Where does Ira often take long breaks?
qa.a: In the stairwell.

qa.q: What was Ira scared of, according to what she finally shared?
qa.a: She was scared she won't cope in the new place, with racing thoughts at night and a tight chest.

qa.q: Which of Darshan's choices made it easier for Ira to open up?
qa.a: Darshan spoke to her privately and made clear the concern was about her, not her work.

qa.q: How might Darshan have seen Ira's bright 'All good!' before the quiet word?
qa.a: Darshan likely sensed it was too bright to match the fast breathing and gripped table, and worried that Ira was struggling.

grounding: A supervisor notices a young adult in a new city hiding racing thoughts, tight chest and fear of not coping, and supports her in sharing and seeking professional help.

passage: 14 August, hostel room, Delhi Third week of college. Everyone thinks I'm settling in fine. I post photos of the canteen and smile at orientation. Inside, my thoughts go a hundred miles an hour. What if I fail the first test? What if I've made a mistake coming this far? Last night my chest felt so tight I sat on the bathroom floor till two. I didn't tell Amma. She'll panic. But today I called Swati Di. I told her everything, even the bathroom floor. She didn't laugh. She said, "Getting help early is the strong thing to do." She stayed on the call while I filled in the campus counselling form, and she made me promise to see the campus doctor about my chest too. Appointment is Friday. I feel lighter already. - Suraj

qa.a: On the bathroom floor.

qa.q: Why did Suraj not tell Amma?
qa.a: Suraj worried that Amma would panic.

qa.a: Suraj shared everything, and with Swati Di's support filled in the counselling form and promised to see the campus doctor.

qa.q: How might Swati Di feel after this call?
qa.a: She may feel worried for Suraj but glad Suraj told her and took early steps toward help.

passage:
Dear Sonali,
I've been in Bengaluru for five weeks now, and I keep telling everyone the new job is "great." It isn't great. Not the job, the job is fine. It's me.
Every morning in the metro my thoughts race: What if I mess up the client call? What if they realise they hired the wrong person? My chest goes tight. At lunch I smile and nod and then cry in the washroom.
I haven't told anyone at work. I've barely told Mum.
But you always said telling someone is half the battle. So I'm telling you. And tomorrow I have an appointment with a counsellor through the office helpline. I booked it last night before I could chicken out.
Wish me luck?
Elizabeth

qa.a: Elizabeth has been in Bengaluru for five weeks.

qa.q: How has Elizabeth been feeling in the new job?
qa.a: Elizabeth has felt anxious and overwhelmed, with racing thoughts and a tight chest, while hiding it behind smiles.

qa.a: Sharing it honestly with Sonali and booking a counsellor through the office helpline early, before it grows.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Sonali may feel worried but also touched and proud that Elizabeth trusted Sonali with this and took a step to get help.

passage: Alka didi, you asked why I called you at midnight in my first month. So, I'm Divyansh, your kid brother, and I'd just moved to Pune for college, and I was sure I was going to fail. My thoughts raced all night: what if I can't keep up, what if I run out of money for the mess, what if everyone finds out I'm not as smart as they think? My chest felt tight, like a belt was pulled round it. In class I laughed and acted fine. I didn't want to be the weak one. Then that night I called you, and you just listened. The next day I went to the college counselling centre. It wasn't weak. Honestly, it was the bravest thing I did that year.

passage:
Week one: Imran, twenty-one, started his first job in Chennai. He didn't know the language well, the office was huge, and every night his thoughts raced. What if I can't do this? What if I have to go home? At work he smiled and said, "All good."
Week two: On the crowded train one morning his chest went tight and he got off two stops early, shaking. At lunch his colleague Keerthana asked, "You okay? You look pale." For once he didn't say fine. "Not really." She listened, then showed him the company's free counselling line.
Week four: Imran has had two sessions. He still worries, but he knows what's happening in his body. He told Keerthana, "Asking was the strongest thing I've done here."

passage:
Sharmila, you're packing for Bengaluru and pretending you're fine. Your Bidisha Pishi knows that face; I wore it at twenty-two, when I moved to Delhi for my first job.
The first week, my thoughts raced all night. My chest felt tight on the metro. I was sure I'd be found out and sent home. I told your grandmother on the phone that everything was wonderful.
One evening my roommate Lata found me sitting on the bathroom floor, breathing fast. She didn't laugh. She sat down with me and waited. Then she said, "My college had a counsellor. Your office must have something too."
It took me three days to email them. It was the bravest email I ever wrote. I went for a few months, and it helped a lot.
So, my girl. If Bengaluru feels like that, tell someone early. Call me. It's not weakness.

qa.q: Who found Pishi sitting on the bathroom floor?
qa.a: Her roommate Lata.

qa.q: How did young Bidisha feel in the first week in Delhi?
qa.a: She felt afraid and overwhelmed, with racing thoughts and a tight chest, sure she'd be found out and sent home.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped young Bidisha cope?
qa.a: Lata's calm support and the push to use the office counsellor; emailing them early, though scary, made a real difference.

qa.q: How might Lata have felt finding her roommate on the floor?
qa.a: Lata was likely worried but steady, choosing to sit with her and suggest help instead of laughing.

grounding: Bidisha Pishi tells her niece how, new in a city and job, she hid racing thoughts and fear until sharing and seeking a counsellor early helped.
